title: "Investing in Artificial General Intelligence"
date: today
date-format: long
format:
  pdf:
    output-file: ai_lab_investment_blind_full.pdf
    keep-tex: true
    linestretch: 1.5
    latex-clean: false
abstract: |
  Frontier AI laboratories racing toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) face uncertain timing of transformative demand.
  They must decide how much irreversible capacity to build, and how to split it between inference (current revenue) and training (future capability).
  I develop a real-options model with regime switching, duopoly competition, endogenous default risk, and diminishing returns calibrated to AI scaling laws.
  The model delivers analytical investment triggers for the single firm and a semi-analytical duopoly preemption equilibrium in which competition compresses investment timing while the training fraction is pinned down by beliefs about AI timelines rather than by competitive position.
  A "faith-based survival" mechanism emerges: training raises the expected post-AGI continuation value, lowering the default boundary---the hope of AGI keeps the firm alive, though that hope is worthless to creditors in bankruptcy.
  An asymmetric dilemma arises: conservative underinvestment is costlier in expected value, but aggressive overinvestment carries substantially higher tail default risk.
  Calibration to four AI lab archetypes illustrates how heterogeneity in beliefs about AI timelines drives cross-sectional variation in investment behavior.
keywords:
  - real options
  - irreversible capacity investment
  - artificial intelligence
  - duopoly preemption
  - default risk
